chapter: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
title: Jelly Roll's published account of the Spikes brothers; Henry Starr replaces him
summary: Spikes reacts to Lomax's quote about Johnny and Reb, and tells of Jelly Roll quitting abruptly in Oakland over Anita, replaced by Henry Starr.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Page 174 of the Jelly Roll book. Okay, you reading...

"It actually came about this way. I was in the music publishing...I was in the music publishing business with Reb and Johnny when I had...met...whom I had met on the stage in the old days. Johnny played piano and Reb, sax. They could read but had no ideas. [laughs] Occasionally I condescended to play with these cornfed musicians. Two of our early tunes became big hits and made the Spikes brothers famous. The first, Someday Sweetheart..." [laughs] and it goes on to tell all about Kid North and all. Oh, you got a lot of stuff in here that he... you know, he was just one of them kinda guys now...George Brown and...
You actually...you wrote "Someday Sweetheart" in what year?

1919. But it didn't become famous till about 1924...'25, you know. [continuing to read Mister Jelly Roll] ..."my luck in California..." Oh, gee whiz. He just wanted to...oh, a lot of this stuff is...uh, I like to wonder if he tell anything about me...how he met me in Oklahoma. I just glancing through this thing [inaudible] ...playing with us and a man in Oakland, and this Anita ran off from him and sent him a telegram, "When you get this telegram, I'll be crossing the Canadian line goin' to Canada." That was about eight o'clock, and by twelve o'clock, he was on the train. Got right up and quit--quit us right in the middle of the night--and he had to go get his woman, you know, so we got another...sent out of town and got a little local boy that was playin' out there named Henry Starr. You heard of Henry Starr?

Well, Henry Starr--we got him to come down, and he played with us. He had never played...uh...uh...in a, you know...in a cabaret or anything at that time, you know. And that started him, and he got to be...have quite a name there. He became kinda famous up there. I don't know where I got all this stuff out of. He got a name--quite a name--after that. Henry Starr. And he worked a lot. Well, I guess that's about all, ain't it?
